items.prompt: When does threat modeling happen in this unit's approach?
choices: Right after the code is released
While the design is still on paper
Once the first incident has been closed out
items.explanation: It is a design-time activity, done before there is code to patch.

items.prompt: Which team spent 30 minutes asking what could go wrong before writing its design doc?
choices: Halcyon
Neither team did
Meridian
items.explanation: Meridian did the pass; Halcyon went straight to the document.

items.prompt: Using the unit's assumed figures, what does a design-time fix cost?
choices: $50 of two engineers' time
$800 including a retest
$45,000 including customer calls
items.explanation: Design-time catch is the cheapest stage at $50 in the demo's assumptions.

items.prompt: Who got the surprise pentest finding four months after launch?
choices: Meridian, which had an allowlist
Both teams, on the same day
Halcyon, which had no security section
items.explanation: Halcyon's gap survived because no one asked the question early.

items.prompt: What does shift-left mean?
choices: Catching a problem at an earlier stage
Moving every automated test into production use
Handing security work to another team
items.explanation: Left is earlier on the lifecycle timeline; earlier catches cost less.

items.prompt: Was the upload gap different between the two teams?
choices: Yes, Halcyon's was harder to fix
No, it was the same gap
Yes, Meridian's was much larger
items.explanation: Only the catch time differed; Meridian closed it before building.

items.prompt: What was wrong with Halcyon's upload?
choices: It took any type and served it from the app's own address
It refused every PDF that students tried to submit for marking
It kept files only on the student's laptop
items.explanation: Any extension plus same-origin serving let a disguised .html file run in other users' sessions.

items.prompt: Why did the two features look identical on day one?
choices: Both teams ran the very same scans
Halcyon's code was reviewed for twice as long
Nothing breaks visibly until someone probes
items.explanation: A missing protection is invisible until an attacker or tester looks.

items.prompt: With the unit's assumed figures, how many times dearer is a production fix than the design-time fix?
choices: 16 times, since $800 divided by $50 is 16
90 times, since $4,500 divided by $50 is 90
900 times, since $45,000 divided by $50 is 900
9,000 times, since $450,000 divided by $50 is 9,000
items.explanation: 45,000 / 50 = 900. The 16x figure is the security-testing stage, not production.
items.reference:
Same gap, three catch points (assumed figures)
design threat model: $50 (1x)
security testing or review: $800 (16x)
production incident: $45,000 (900x)
the gap itself never changed
Why: only the number of stages the gap survives changes the price, and most of that price is coordination, not code.
items.learnMore:
Why later is dearer

A fix at design time is an edit to a diagram. After release it is a code change plus a rollout, an emergency, and a conversation with customers. The figures used in this unit are illustrative assumptions from its demo, not measured industry data.

Common mistake

Assuming the late fix is expensive because the code change is hard. The change is often an afternoon; the surrounding coordination is the cost.
items.reflection: Think of a household or personal project where a quick check at the planning stage would have saved a much bigger repair later. What made the early check feel skippable at the time?

items.prompt: A lead says: 'A pentest will find it anyway, so skip the threat model.' Which reply is strongest?
choices: It will find it, but later, so the same gap costs more to fix
It will find it, so the threat model adds nothing of value at all
It cannot find it, because tests only cover known bugs
It will find it, but only if the code is rewritten first
items.explanation: Testing does catch the gap, but at a stage where it costs 16x the design-time fix under the unit's assumptions.

items.prompt: What does secure by default mean?
choices: Every setting is locked after launch
The untouched setup is already the safe one
Security tools come pre-installed on all hosts
items.explanation: It is about the behavior when no one configures anything.

items.prompt: A new IAM role should begin with which permissions?
choices: Read access to every resource in the account
Admin, until it is narrowed later
None, plus one named grant at a time
items.explanation: Restrictive default: zero permissions, grants added by name.

items.prompt: A new upload field should accept which file types at first?
choices: None until an allowlist exists
Any type until a blocklist exists
Only images, and nothing else ever
items.explanation: Deny by default means nothing passes without an explicit allow.

items.prompt: A new endpoint skips login only when what holds?
choices: Nobody remembered to protect it
It currently has very few users
It is explicitly marked public
items.explanation: The unusual case, public, must be typed out loud.

items.prompt: What does 'fails open' mean?
choices: A missed step leaves access available
A missed step shuts down the whole system
A failed deploy reopens the ticket
items.explanation: Fail open means the error side is access, the unsafe side.

items.prompt: Is 'someone did nothing' a rare event in real code?
choices: Yes, every field gets touched
No, it is the norm
Only on small teams
items.explanation: Most fields stay at their defaults most of the time.

items.prompt: Which default makes a forgotten allowlist harmless?
choices: Restrictive: nothing is accepted without one
Permissive: everything is accepted unless blocked
Neutral: the first request decides it
items.explanation: A forgotten step then leaves the field closed, not open.

items.prompt: What is a permissive default?
choices: Closed unless someone later opens it up
Open only during the weekend deploys
Open unless someone later restricts it
items.explanation: Permissive means the unconfigured state allows access.

items.prompt: An endpoint needs `public: true` to skip login. A developer forgets the flag. What is the outcome?
choices: It requires login: annoying, but still protected
It is open to the public until a scan finds it
It shuts down every other endpoint on the service
It logs a warning and then serves without login
items.explanation: Restrictive default: the forgotten step leaves the endpoint closed, which is the cheaper mistake.
items.reference:
Which way does a forgotten step fail?
permissive default: forgotten step leaves it open
restrictive default: forgotten step leaves it closed
upload field: no types until an allowlist exists
endpoint: login required unless marked public
Why: doing nothing is the most common thing a team does, so the do-nothing result should be the safe one.
items.learnMore:
Fail open versus fail closed

Secure by default does not remove configuration work. It chooses the direction a missed step falls in. A closed mistake is a ticket; an open mistake is an incident.

Common mistake

Treating it as 'the same work, just earlier'. The point is the failure direction, not the effort total.
items.reflection: Where in your own routines does doing nothing leave something open (a spare key, a shared password, an unlocked door)? What would a closed-by-default version look like?

items.prompt: A teammate says secure by default only moves configuration earlier. What does it actually change?
choices: The total effort, which drops to nearly nothing
Who is allowed to approve the design review
The number of threats the design must list
The direction a missed step fails in
items.explanation: Work may stay similar; failing closed instead of open is the real gain.

items.prompt: A framework makes every new storage bucket readable by any signed-in user until restricted. How is this best described?
choices: Secure by default, since sign-in is required before any read happens
Permissive by default; start private and grant access by name
Restrictive, because anonymous users are still blocked
Neutral, since the admin can change it afterwards
items.explanation: Any unconfigured bucket is exposed to every signed-in user; the safe design starts private.

items.prompt: What does a data-flow diagram show?
choices: Who originally wrote each part of the code
How data moves between system parts
How fast each part responds
items.explanation: A DFD is a map of data movement with trust zones marked.

items.prompt: What is a trust boundary?
choices: A firewall around the whole network
A list of approved vendors only
A line where trust level changes
items.explanation: Crossing it means data moves between different trust levels.

items.prompt: Which arrow is riskiest in the upload diagram?
choices: Browser to API
Queue to storage after the scan
CDN to the instructor's browser
items.explanation: It is the only arrow accepting bytes from a not-yet-trusted party.

items.prompt: Where do threats cluster in a diagram?
choices: In the exact middle of every box
Only at the database boxes
At arrows that cross a trust boundary
items.explanation: Crossings are where trust changes.

items.prompt: Why draw before listing threats?
choices: The team needs a shared picture first
Drawings replace the written threat list entirely
Auditors demand a drawing first
items.explanation: Everyone must agree what the system is before asking what can go wrong.

items.prompt: Is the student's browser trusted?
choices: Yes, it is part of the app
No, it is untrusted input
Only after the student logs in
items.explanation: Anything the system does not control is untrusted input.

items.prompt: What is the first step of a threat-model pass?
choices: Draw the system and mark trust changes
Buy and configure a vulnerability scanner
Write the final incident report
items.explanation: Describe the system before analysing it.

items.prompt: What do the shaded zones in the diagram represent?
choices: Parts owned by different teams
Parts running on different servers
Parts at the same trust level
items.explanation: Colour marks trust level, not ownership or hardware.

items.prompt: In the upload diagram, which arrow deserves the most scrutiny, and why?
choices: API to storage, because storage is the largest and busiest component here
CDN to instructor, because it is the final arrow
Browser to API, because it accepts input from a not-yet-trusted party
Queue to storage, because it has the most data
items.explanation: Risk comes from where trust changes, not size or position in the sequence.
items.reference:
Reading a data-flow diagram
boxes: parts of the system
arrows: data moving between parts
shaded zones: who trusts whom
arrows crossing zones: where threats cluster
Why: a shared picture of the system has to exist before anyone can ask what could go wrong with it.
items.learnMore:
Why boundaries, not boxes

A threat needs somewhere to enter. Inside one zone the parts already trust each other; at a crossing the system accepts something from a party it trusts less. That is where checks belong.

Common mistake

Treating every box as equally risky. Effort is better spent at the crossings than in the middle of a zone.
items.reflection: Pick a building you know. Where are its trust boundaries (front door, side door, loading dock), and which crossing gets the least checking?

items.prompt: A team adds a webhook that receives data from a payment provider into the API. What changes in the diagram?
choices: A new arrow crossing from an untrusted zone into the app, to be checked
Nothing, since payment providers are always trusted
Only the storage box changes, to hold the payments
The whole diagram is replaced with a new one
items.explanation: Any new input path from outside is a new crossing and needs the same questions.

items.prompt: Two services inside the same app boundary exchange data. Compared with the browser-to-API arrow, how much threat scrutiny does that arrow usually need?
choices: More, because internal traffic is invisible to scanners
None, since inside a boundary nothing can go wrong
The same, because every arrow is equally risky
Less, because trust does not change, though not zero
items.explanation: Without a change in trust the exposure is lower, but a compromised neighbour can still misbehave.

items.prompt: How many STRIDE categories are there?
choices: Three, one for each tier
Six, one for each letter
Ten, one for each layer
items.explanation: S, T, R, I, D, E.

items.prompt: Spoofing asks which question?
choices: Can the system be made slow?
Can the same record be logged twice by mistake?
Can someone pretend to be another user?
items.explanation: Spoofing is about false identity.

items.prompt: Tampering asks which question?
choices: Can data be changed unexpectedly?
Can a user forget their password again?
Can a page load a bit faster?
items.explanation: Tampering is unauthorized modification.

items.prompt: Repudiation is about what?
choices: A file that is stored without encryption
A user who forgot to log out
An action nobody can prove who did
items.explanation: Without records, the actor can deny the action.

items.prompt: Guessing another student's file address is which category?
choices: Information disclosure
Denial of service
Elevation of privilege abuse
items.explanation: Data reaches someone who should not see it.

items.prompt: Filling storage with huge uploads is which category?
choices: Tampering with data
Denial of service
Repudiation of uploads
items.explanation: The goal is making the system unusable for others.

items.prompt: A file running with the service's own privileges is which category?
choices: Elevation of privilege
Information disclosure
Denial of service
items.explanation: Access grew beyond what the action should have.

items.prompt: Do all six categories apply equally to every element?
choices: Yes, each must produce a threat
No, so only three of them are ever asked in practice
No, but asking all six avoids blind spots
items.explanation: Some answers are 'not applicable'; asking is what matters.

items.prompt: A forged content-type header disguises a script as a PDF. Which STRIDE category is that?
choices: Spoofing
Repudiation
Elevation of privilege
Tampering
items.explanation: The data is altered to be something the system did not expect.
items.reference:
The six STRIDE questions
Spoofing: can someone pretend to be someone else?
Tampering: can data be changed unexpectedly?
Repudiation: can an action be denied for lack of proof?
Information disclosure: can data leak to the wrong party?
Denial of service: can use be blocked for others?
Elevation of privilege: can access grow beyond intent?
Why: six fixed questions per crossing stop a real threat from being missed because nobody thought of that angle.
items.learnMore:
Questions, not a score

STRIDE does not rank threats. It guarantees each angle is asked once at each crossing. The answer for a given crossing may well be 'not applicable', which is a result too.

Common mistake

Hunting for exactly one threat per letter. Some crossings have several for one letter and none for another.
items.reflection: Take a shared account at home (streaming, banking, a house key). Which STRIDE question worries you most about it, and what would answer it?

items.prompt: A malicious file arrives and the team cannot tell which account sent it. Which category?
choices: Tampering
Repudiation
Information disclosure
Denial of service
items.explanation: No proof of who acted, so the actor can deny it.

Information disclosure

items.prompt: Where does the threat list go after the STRIDE pass?
choices: Into a private note on someone's laptop
Into the design doc's security section
Into the production log files
items.explanation: Written into the document so the review can see it.

items.prompt: Which review gate checks the security section?
choices: A yearly audit by outside auditors
The customer support team's weekly review
The one that checks scalability and cost
items.explanation: It sits beside the other design sections.

items.prompt: Why did Meridian do the pass reliably?
choices: Its template required it
Its engineers were more careful
Its sprint simply had more days
items.explanation: The template enforced the habit; individuals were not the difference.

items.prompt: How long should a pass for a feature this size take?
choices: Several weeks of workshops
A full quarter of dedicated work
About one focused 30-minute session
items.explanation: If it cannot be time-boxed it gets skipped.

items.prompt: Does a copy tweak need a full STRIDE pass?
choices: No, it crosses no new boundary
Yes, because every change does
Only when it ships on a Friday
items.explanation: Scope the ask to changes with a new input, flow or boundary.

items.prompt: If review finds a gap, what happens?
choices: The build starts anyway, with a note
The design goes back to draft
The gap moves to next sprint's wiki
items.explanation: The gate loops until gaps are closed or accepted.

items.prompt: Why write the security section before building?
choices: Changing a design costs less than changing code
Code can never be security-tested after it is written
Reviewers refuse to read any code
items.explanation: Design-time catches cost less.

items.prompt: What should a pass be compared against when talking to a product owner?
choices: The price of a replacement laptop
The total size of the codebase
The cost of a later emergency fix
items.explanation: Price the alternative, not only the up-front time.

items.prompt: Why does a required template section beat telling engineers to be more careful?
choices: It lets reviewers skip reading the design doc
It works on rushed days, when good habits slip
It removes the need for any threat analysis
It makes the section shorter than other sections
items.explanation: Enforcement by process survives pressure; good intentions do not.
items.reference:
From threat list to gate
draft design and diagram
STRIDE pass at each crossing
'Security considerations' section in the doc
design review, same gate as scalability
gaps found: back to draft
Why: a required section survives deadline days; an optional habit does not.
items.learnMore:
A process, not a hero

Meridian was not made of more careful people. Its template required the section before approval, so the habit happened on busy days too. Proportion keeps it sustainable: only changes with a new input, data flow or boundary need a pass.

Common mistake

Making the pass mandatory for every edit. A tax on trivial changes erodes goodwill for the practice itself.
items.reflection: Think of a checklist you rely on (packing, deploying, cooking). What made it work on a rushed day, and what would have made you skip it?

items.prompt: Which change most clearly needs a STRIDE pass?
choices: A button's colour changed from blue to green
A variable renamed inside one internal function
A log line reworded for clearer wording
A new text field shown back to other users
items.explanation: A new user-controlled input crosses a trust boundary; the others add none.

items.prompt: A product owner resists a 30-minute pass. Which framing is most useful?
choices: Say the pass is required by the security team
30 minutes now versus an emergency fix later
Promise it will never delay a single ship date
Offer to do it after the feature launches
items.explanation: The honest comparison is cost now versus the larger cost of the same gap later.

items.prompt: What stops a student guessing another's file address?
choices: A longer account password
Random storage names
A larger file size limit
items.explanation: Unpredictable names cannot be enumerated.

items.prompt: What is the quarantine prefix for?
choices: Archiving files that are too old
Compressing files that are far too large to store
Holding files until the scan clears them
items.explanation: Only scanned files are promoted to servable storage.

items.prompt: How long do signed links live in this design?
choices: 10 minutes
10 days
Until the course ends
items.explanation: Short-lived links limit the damage of a leak.

items.prompt: Which row does the audit log answer?
choices: Denial of service: too many uploads
Tampering: the wrong file type
Repudiation: who uploaded this?
items.explanation: The log supplies the proof of who acted.

items.prompt: What does an extension allowlist do?
choices: Rejects every type not listed
Accepts every type not blocked
Scans every file for malware
items.explanation: Deny by default: only listed types pass.

items.prompt: Why have a file size cap?
choices: To make files load more slowly
To stop uploads exhausting storage
To hide original file names
items.explanation: It closes the denial-of-service row for size.

items.prompt: Why not trust the content-type header the browser sends?
choices: The sender controls it and can forge it
It is always blank on uploads
Servers are unable to read any request headers
items.explanation: Checks must happen on the server, on the content.

items.prompt: Why must a course-assignment check run before a link is issued?
choices: To speed up each file download
To compress the file before it is sent out
To stop non-assigned users getting links
items.explanation: It closes the spoofing row for link requests.

items.prompt: A file is served before the malware scan finishes. Which control closes that row?
choices: Signed links that expire after ten minutes
Random, non-sequential storage names
Quarantine until the scan clears
A per-account upload rate limit
items.explanation: The row is about serving timing, which only holding files back controls.
items.reference:
Threat to mitigation
tampering at upload: allowlist + server-side content check
served before scan: quarantine, then promote
guessable file name: random storage names
leaked link: 10-minute, single-object links
no proof of sender: audit log of every upload
Why: each row of the table names the control that closes it, so no control is a guess.
items.learnMore:
One threat, one named control

A mitigation without a row is decoration, and a row without a mitigation is an open risk. Pairing them keeps the design honest and makes later changes reviewable.

Common mistake

Believing one strong control covers several rows. Random names do nothing about a script in an allowed file type.

items.prompt: Implement `canDo(grants, role, action)`. `grants` maps a role name to an array of allowed actions. Return true only if the role exists and lists the action. An unknown role is not allowed.
items.explanation: An unknown role has no array, so the check returns false before looking for the action. Only an exact listed action returns true.

items.prompt: Implement `isPublic(endpoint)`. Return true only if `endpoint.public` is exactly `true`. Anything else, including a missing field or the string "true", means not public.
items.explanation: Strict equality means only the real boolean true opens the endpoint. A missing field or a string falls through to false.

items.prompt: Implement `visibility(setting)`. Return "public" only if `setting` is exactly the string "public". For anything else (undefined, other strings, other types) return "private".
items.explanation: Only an exact match opens the setting. A typo, a different case or a missing value all land on private.

items.prompt: Implement `withinLimit(bytes, maxBytes)`. Return true only if `bytes` is a whole number greater than 0 and not above `maxBytes`.
items.explanation: Each condition must hold for true. Zero, fractions and values over the limit each fail one condition.

items.prompt: Implement `isFresh(issuedAt, now, ttlSeconds)`. A link is valid only while `0 <= now - issuedAt < ttlSeconds`. Anything else is false.
items.explanation: A link issued in the future gives a negative age and fails. A link exactly at its time limit is already expired because the check is strictly less than.

items.prompt: Implement `isAllowedExtension(filename, allowed)`. `allowed` is an array of lowercase extensions such as ".pdf". Return true only if the filename's last dot-suffix, lowercased, is in the list. A name with no dot is not allowed.
items.explanation: The last dot-suffix is lowercased and looked up in the list. A name without a dot returns false before any lookup.

items.prompt: Implement `isUploadAllowed(filename, sizeBytes, allowed, maxBytes)`. Return true only if (a) the LAST extension, lowercased, is in `allowed` (so "a.pdf.html" is judged as ".html"), (b) the name has a real extension (a name that is only an extension such as ".pdf", or has no dot, is not allowed), and (c) `sizeBytes` is a whole number from 1 up to `maxBytes`.
items.explanation: Using the last dot means a disguised double extension is judged by its real, final suffix. A dot at position 0 or none at all means no usable extension, and the size must be a positive whole number within the cap.
items.reference:
Write the closed case first
unknown role: no grants, so false
missing field: treat as not allowed
expired or malformed: false
only an exact match returns true
Why: when code is deny by default, the path nobody wrote lands on the safe side.
items.learnMore:
Default to false

Start from a function that returns false and add exactly one condition under which it returns true. Missing keys, wrong types and boundary values then fail safely instead of passing by accident.

Common mistake

Returning true when a lookup finds nothing. A missing rule should mean no.
items.reflection: Think of a rule you follow (a house rule, a store policy). What happens when a case arises that nobody planned for, and does the rule fail open or closed?

items.prompt: Implement `canAccess(policy, role, action)`. `policy` maps a role to `{ allow: [...], deny: [...] }`. Return true only if the role exists, the action is in its `allow` list, and it is NOT in its `deny` list. A deny always wins. A missing `allow` or `deny` list counts as empty.
items.explanation: An unknown role stops at false. The deny list is checked before the allow list so a deny always wins, and a missing list is treated as empty rather than as permission.

items.prompt: Implement `isLinkValid(link, now, objectKey)`. `link` is `{ key, expiresAt }` with times in seconds. Return true only if `link` exists, `link.key` equals `objectKey`, and `now` is a number strictly less than `link.expiresAt`. A missing link or a non-numeric time is false.
items.explanation: Every check fails closed: no link, a link for another object, or a non-numeric time all return false. Expiry uses a strict comparison, so a link is dead at its exact limit.
